title: RAID: Many Disks, One Logical Drive
topic: RAID — combining several disks to trade capacity for speed (striping, RAID-0), redundancy (mirroring, RAID-1), or both (parity, RAID-5). Visualises a block landing across multiple disks and what happens when one disk dies.

beats.narration: A single disk gives you one shot at not failing. RAID groups several disks behind one logical drive and trades off speed, capacity, and survival.

elements.content: Three layouts. Same disks. Different tradeoffs.

beats.narration: RAID zero splits each block across all the disks. Reads and writes go in parallel, so throughput multiplies. But one disk dies and the whole array is lost.

elements.content: A block A splits into stripes A0, A1, A2, A3 and slides into four disks D0..D3 in parallel; later one disk is crossed out — all of A is gone

beats.narration: RAID one mirrors every block onto two disks. You lose half your capacity, but a single disk failure leaves a complete copy behind.

elements.content: Block A duplicates into two disks D0 and D1 along parallel arrows; one disk fails — block still readable from the other

beats.narration: RAID five stripes data across all the disks plus one parity stripe — the bitwise xor of the others. Lose any single disk, and the missing stripe can be xor'd back from what's left.

elements.content: Four disks. Row shows stripes A0, A1, A2 plus parity Ap = A0 ⊕ A1 ⊕ A2; one disk crossed out and the lost stripe gets reconstructed by xor-ing the others; arrows show the recompute

beats.narration: RAID zero buys speed and gambles. RAID one buys safety and pays half. RAID five buys both and pays one disk out of however many you have.
